https://daryo.uz/en/2026/10/23/uzbekista.body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan introduces new financial sanctions for violations of water withdrawal regulations Uzbekistan has introduced financial sanctions for legal entities violating water withdrawal regulations, with a first-offense warning system taking effect on January 1, 2027, penalties increasing fivefold for repeated violations, and provisions allowing a 50% reduction for voluntary payment or installment payments over six months. Yesterday, 18:01 3 min read 1 052 views 0 comments 0 Source: “Daryo” / Farrux Aliyev Uzbekistan has established procedures for imposing financial sanctions on legal entities that violate water withdrawal regulations in agriculture, fisheries, industry, energy and domestic water use. The measures are outlined in a government resolution dated October 21. Under the resolution, a warning system for first-time violations will take effect on January 1, 2027, while repeated violations may result in financial sanctions increased fivefold. The resolution identifies several types of violations related to water withdrawal and usage. These include: Withdrawing water in excess of established limits. Using water without a contract or special permit. Failing to equip water withdrawal points with metering and management devices. Withdrawing water without authorization. Legal entities found responsible for these violations will be subject to the procedures established under the resolution. Starting January 1, 2027, Uzbekistan will introduce a "warning for the first offense" principle for legal entities. The provision will apply when a legal entity commits a violation for the first time within a year, provided that the violation does not cause harm to human life or health or damage to another person's property. In such cases, the responsible inspectorate will issue a warning through the suvnazorat.uz platform and provide instructions on correcting the identified violation. The legal entity will have 10 days to comply with the instructions. If the requirements are not fulfilled within that period, financial sanctions will be imposed. The amount of financial sanctions will be determined using the base calculation amount (BCA) for every 1,000 cubic meters of water. The calculation will apply the percentages established under Article 164 of Uzbekistan's Water Code. The resolution also introduces higher penalties for repeated violations. If a legal entity commits another violation within one year after a financial sanction has been imposed, the amount of the sanction will be increased fivefold. The resolution provides a mechanism allowing legal entities to reduce the amount payable if they settle sanctions voluntarily. If a legal entity pays 50% of the financial sanction within one month of receiving the relevant decision and calculation, it will be exempted from paying the remaining 50%. The document also allows sanctions to be paid in installments over six months. Under this arrangement, the legal entity must pay at least one-sixth of the total sanction amount each month. If a legal entity does not make the required voluntary payment within one month, the inspectorate will apply to the court. The resolution also establishes procedures for appealing financial sanctions. If an appeal is filed against a sanction, its enforcement will be suspended until the appeal has been reviewed. The resolution sets out requirements for returning payments collected under sanctions that are subsequently found to be unlawful or groundless. If a court determines that a financial sanction was imposed unlawfully or without sufficient grounds, the amount paid must be refunded within 15 days. If the refund is delayed, interest will accrue for each day of delay at a rate equal to one three-hundredth (1/300) of the Central Bank's base rate. Earlier, Uzbekistan approved procedures allowing entrepreneurs to lease land from the water fund through electronic auctions. The measures apply to land created as a result of converting open collector-drainage networks into closed drainage systems. # Environmental Law # Financial Penalties # Government Resolution # Regulatory Enforcement # Water Resource Management # uzbekistan Telegram channel @daryo_eng Subscribe What do you think? https://kun.uz/en/news/2026/10/23/uzbeki.body: The agreement was reached at the 10th meeting of the Uzbekistan–India Joint Working Group on Counterterrorism, held in New Delhi on October 22, 2026, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said . The meeting was co-chaired by Suhel Ajaz Khan, India’s Additional Secretary responsible for counterterrorism, and Gulomjon Pirimkulov, head of the department for cooperation with South Asian, Middle Eastern and African countries at Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The delegations reviewed threats posed by terrorist groups globally and in their respective regions, exchanging views on existing and emerging challenges. Discussions covered efforts to counter extremism and radicalization, disrupt terrorist financing, prevent the use of technology for terrorist purposes, and address links between terrorism and transnational organized crime. Both sides also considered ways to deepen bilateral cooperation through intelligence and information sharing, capacity-building and exchanges of best practices, as well as closer coordination between their relevant agencies. Uzbekistan and India reaffirmed their commitment to working together in multilateral forums, including the United Nations, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization’s Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure and the Eurasian Group on Combating Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism. The next meeting of the joint working group will be held in Uzbekistan, with the date to be agreed by both sides.

https://kz.kursiv.media/en/2026-10-23/en.body: Photo: Unsplash, photo editor: Adelina Mamedova Kazakhstan and China may launch a pilot project for autonomous cargo transportation. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport has signed a memorandum of understanding with China TransInfo Group. The parties signed the document at the New Silk Way international business forum, which focuses on the transport industry. The memorandum covers autonomous transport and the digitalization of the transport sector. «The document lays the groundwork for long-term cooperation in introducing autonomous technologies and digital solutions in the transport sector,» the ministry noted. The ministry added that Kazakhstan and Russia implemented a pilot project involving autonomous trucks on the Astana-Moscow route this year. The next step could be to launch a similar project with China along sections of international transport corridors. In May 2026, the transport ministries of Kazakhstan and Russia, together with KAMAZ, successfully launched autonomous trucks on the Astana-Moscow route. The trucks crossed the border simultaneously at the Zhanazhol checkpoint and continued to their destinations in autonomous mode. The trucks completed the approximately 3,000-kilometer route without drivers. The new technology cut travel time by more than half, allowing the journey to be completed in just two days. https://www.azernews.az/business/266093..body: Azerbaijan–Ukraine trade exceeds $407 million as bilateral commerce grows for third year 23 October 2026 19:59 (UTC+04:00) Akbar Novruz Read more Trade turnover between Azerbaijan and Ukraine reached $407.4 million in January–September 2026, representing an increase of 8.7% compared with the corresponding period last year, according to the State Customs Committee. During the first nine months of the year, Azerbaijan exported goods worth $190.9 million to Ukraine, while imports from Ukraine amounted to $216.4 million. As a result, Azerbaijan recorded a trade deficit of approximately $25.5 million with Ukraine during the reporting period. The latest figures indicate continued growth in bilateral trade following increases recorded in both 2024 and 2025. According to previously published customs statistics, trade turnover between Azerbaijan and Ukraine stood at approximately $342.9 million in January–September 2024. The figure increased by 9.2% to $374.5 million during the corresponding period of 2025, with Azerbaijani exports reaching $169 million and imports from Ukraine totalling approximately $205.6 million. In the first nine months of 2025, Azerbaijan's non-oil and gas exports to Ukraine also increased by 83.6% year-on-year to $147.3 million. Major exported products included agricultural goods, fruit juices, tea, mineral fertilisers and petroleum-related products. Comparing the latest figures with those from 2025, Azerbaijan's exports to Ukraine increased by approximately 13%, while imports grew by around 5.3%. The trade relationship has also remained an important subject of bilateral economic discussions. During an August 2026 meeting in Kyiv, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Ukraine was interested in restoring trade with Azerbaijan to pre-war levels. He noted that bilateral trade had reached approximately $600 million on an annual basis, compared with $922.4 million recorded in 2021. The two countries also agreed to pursue further economic cooperation, including through their bilateral intergovernmental commission. Tags: trade with Azerbaijan trade relations Azerbaijan-Ukraine

https://24.kg/en/article/kyrgyzstans-fin.body: Kyrgyzstan’s Ministry of Finance has been granted expanded powers in managing public funds and debt obligations, as well as overseeing budget spending. The Cabinet of Ministers adopted Resolution No. 716 on October 22, 2026. Under the document, the ministry will be able to develop and introduce new financial instruments, including mechanisms for using funds from the state debt relief account. The ministry will also develop a methodology for assessing the effectiveness of public investment projects, conduct financial and economic analyses of investment initiatives, and monitor the implementation of state investment programs. The document separately outlines the ministry’s responsibilities for managing the Kyrgyz Republic’s Stabilization Fund. In particular, the ministry will ensure that funds are transferred to the fund based on presidential decisions, manage its accounts, and prepare reports on incoming funds and their use. Another change concerns digital oversight of public finances. The ministry has been tasked with creating and developing an electronic audit system that will automatically analyze financial transactions conducted by government agencies and organizations, generate analytical reports, and track financial risks. The ministry must also establish dedicated channels for reporting corruption offenses, including through official websites, secure electronic systems, and hotlines. The amendments will take effect in 10 days.

https://24.kg/en/article/kyrgyzstan-plan.body: Kyrgyzstan plans to eventually build tunnels using its own resources, rather than relying on Chinese companies currently involved in such projects. President Sadyr Japarov said this during a meeting with residents of Nooken district and the town of Mailuu-Suu. The issue was raised by a resident of Kochkor-Ata, who proposed involving domestic engineers, specialists and construction equipment more actively in major infrastructure projects. ❮ ❯ ✏️ Edit 1/2 He said developing the country’s own construction capacity would help keep more funds in Kyrgyzstan, create jobs and build professional expertise. As a first step, he suggested launching several pilot projects. Japarov supported the proposal and spoke about the work of the Ministry of Transport. According to the president, in 2021–2022 the ministry began building and asphalting roads on its own. The country purchased about 1,500 pieces of equipment for this purpose. Previously, the ministry had largely outsourced road construction to contractors, including foreign companies. The authorities are now seeking to develop domestic capabilities, Japarov said. He added that Kyrgyzstan currently asphalt-paves around 2,000 kilometers of roads annually. Tunnels, however, are still being built by Chinese companies. The president attributed this to the lack of the necessary equipment and sufficient experience in Kyrgyzstan. Sadyr Japarov acknowledged that domestic specialists still need to improve the quality of road construction. He said expertise develops gradually and that Kyrgyz professionals would eventually be able to carry out such work to a higher standard.

https://24.kg/article/kyrgyzstan-nachnet.body: Кыргызстан в перспективе рассчитывает самостоятельно строить тоннели, для возведения которых сейчас привлекают китайские компании. Об этом президент Садыр Жапаров заявил во время встречи с жителями Ноокенского района и города Майлуу-Суу. Тема прозвучала после выступления жителя Кочкор-Аты. Он предложил активнее привлекать отечественных инженеров, специалистов и строительную технику к реализации крупных инфраструктурных проектов. ❮ ❯ ✏️ Edit 1/2 Встреча Садыра Жапаров с жителями Ноокенского района и города Майлуу-Суу. Фото администрации президента По мнению мужчины, развитие собственного строительного потенциала позволит оставлять больше средств внутри страны, создавать рабочие места и накапливать профессиональный опыт. В качестве одного из решений он предложил начать с нескольких пилотных проектов. Читайте по теме Садыр Жапаров: Все хотят работать с Китаем, а мы его отвергаем Жапаров поддержал эту идею и рассказал о работе министерства транспорта. По его словам, с 2021–2022 годов ведомство начало самостоятельно строить дороги и асфальтировать их. Для этого республика закупила около 1,5 тысячи единиц техники. Президент отметил, что раньше министерство в основном передавало дорожное строительство подрядчикам, в том числе иностранным компаниям. Теперь власти стремятся развивать собственные возможности. По словам Жапарова, сейчас Кыргызстан ежегодно асфальтирует около 2 тысяч километров дорог. При этом тоннели пока строят китайские компании. Президент объяснил это отсутствием у Кыргызстана необходимой техники и достаточного опыта. Садыр Жапаров признал, что отечественным специалистам еще предстоит совершенствовать качество дорожного строительства. По его мнению, опыт приходит постепенно, и со временем кыргызстанские специалисты смогут выполнять такие работы на более высоком уровне.

https://en.kabar.kg/news/president-zhapa.body: Presidential administration Bishkek, Oct. 23, 2026. /Kabar/. President of Kyrgyzstan Sadyr Zhaparov has signed a decree "On the Approval of the National Program for the Development and Popularization of Chess in the Kyrgyz Republic for 2026–2030." The objective of the decree is to create conditions that facilitate the development and popularization of chess in Kyrgyzstan, promote mass participation in chess across all segments of the population, develop a reserve of athletes, and enhance the competitiveness of Kyrgyz chess players on the international stage. The decree provides for the approval of: 1) The National Program for the Development and Popularization of Chess in the Kyrgyz Republic for 2026–2030; 2) Action plan for the implementation of the National Program for the Development and Popularization of Chess in the Kyrgyz Republic for 2026–2030; 3) The budget for the action plan; 4) A matrix of indicators for monitoring and evaluating the implementation of the National Program. It should be noted that, under the Presidential Decree "On Urgent Measures for the Development and Popularization of Chess in Kyrgyzstan for 2026–2030," signed on June 3, 2026, the development and popularization of chess were designated as a priority area of the Kyrgyz Republic's state social policy. https://www.azernews.az/region/266069.ht.body: Armenia’s future in CSTO could be discussed at Moscow summit 23 October 2026 15:28 (UTC+04:00) Ulviyya Poladova Read more Armenia has effectively withdrawn from the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO). Speaking to journalists, the organization’s Secretary General, Taatbek Masadykov, said that Yerevan continues to receive documents sent to member states for domestic approval. In response, the Armenian side states that it does not participate in discussions or decision-making but does not object to decisions being adopted in a restricted format. He noted that Armenia’s representative attends the weekly meetings of the CSTO Permanent Council and listens to reports. However, the country does not participate in the organization’s main events or military exercises. The Secretary General also did not rule out the possibility that Armenia’s membership could be discussed at a session of the CSTO Collective Security Council scheduled to take place in Moscow on November 11. He added that this could happen if the presiding country or another member state puts forward a relevant proposal. Masadykov linked the current situation to Article 25 of the CSTO Charter. He explained that failure to pay membership contributions and fill quota-based positions could result in the loss of voting rights. Earlier, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan told parliament that he supported Armenia’s removal from the CSTO and would welcome such a development. He also stated that Yerevan did not intend to participate actively in the organization’s activities over the next five years. Armenia had previously announced that it was "freezing" its participation in the CSTO. In December 2024, Pashinyan said that the country’s relations with the organization had passed the point of no return. Tags: Moscow Russia Armenia CSTO Nikol Pashinyan

Tehran has warned neighboring countries against supporting any renewed military campaign. According to the newspaper, the plans envisage a short but intensive military operation. The US and Israeli armed forces have stepped up preparations and are conducting training flights over Iraq to rehearse potential strikes. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel on October 19, CBS News reported, amid discussions about a possible resumption of military operations against Iran. Potential targets include Iran’s nuclear facilities, missile and drone arsenals, and energy infrastructure, according to The New York Times . Some US military planners believe an operation lasting about three days could inflict serious damage on Iran’s economy and increase pressure on Tehran in negotiations. No final decision on new strikes has been made. A White House spokesman said the administration does not comment on military plans “that may or may not exist,” adding that President Donald Trump is keeping all options open to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. Trump previously postponed planned strikes The US and Israel came close to launching a new round of strikes in early October, according to The New York Times . Both militaries had completed preparations and placed aircraft on heightened alert, but Trump postponed the operation shortly before its planned launch. Earlier, The Wall Street Journal , citing US officials, reported that Trump was considering resuming bombing after the November elections. The newspaper said the president had repeatedly delayed a decision on returning to large-scale military operations. Meanwhile, the United States is strengthening its military presence in the Middle East, with additional ships, aircraft and troops being deployed to the region, according to the Wall Street Journal . Iran warns neighboring countries Amid reports of a possible new military campaign, Tehran has stepped up warnings to countries across the Middle East. Feda-Hossein Maleki, a member of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, told Russia’s RIA Novosti news agency that regional countries had been warned not to support the United States if hostilities resume. Maleki said Iran had previously struck US bases in countries whose territory was used for operations against the Islamic Republic. He warned that any new escalation could prompt Tehran to go beyond targeting military bases, adding that countries assisting Washington could be regarded as hostile by Iran. IRGC announces shift toward offensive operations Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesman Hossein Mohebbi has also said Iran’s military doctrine has changed. In an interview with Iran’s Student News Network on October 21, he said that while the country had previously focused primarily on responding to attacks, it was now prepared to take offensive action. “If any country attacks us, we will not only respond, but will also launch an offensive,” IranWire quoted Mohebbi as saying. He said Iran intended to use asymmetric warfare tactics and pursue what he described as “permanent deterrence.” Mohebbi also announced preparations to unveil a new weapon that Iran calls the “father of all bombs.” He did not provide verified technical specifications for the weapon. Iran’s geographic position provides Uzbekistan with an additional route to regional and international markets. The countries are preparing to hold the 17th meeting of their Joint Intergovernmental Commission and an Uzbekistan–Iran Business Forum in Tashkent on November 26–27. The events are expected to provide a platform for advancing joint projects and identifying further opportunities for trade and investment. The latest meeting follows political consultations held in Tehran in August, when the two countries’ foreign ministries discussed strengthening political dialogue, expanding economic cooperation and addressing regional and international issues of mutual interest. https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/10/23/taji.body: Share asia+ Categories Society Tajikistan Format News Published 23.10.2026 17:13 Translations Eng Рус Tajikistan’s Agency for Social Insurance and Pensions says the Asian Development Bank (ADB)’s proposal to raise the retirement age is advisory and does not change the country’s current legislation. In a statement published on Facebook on October 22, the agency said pension eligibility and the conditions for receiving benefits are governed by national law. “Any changes to the retirement age, insurance record and other conditions for the granting of pensions must be considered and adopted in the manner established by the legislation of Tajikistan,” the agency said, adding that changes would take effect only after the relevant legal acts enter into force. The current retirement age in Tajikistan is 58 for women and 63 for men. In a recent report, the ADB recommended that the country consider two options: gradually raising the retirement age for women from 58 to 63, or setting it at 65 for both women and men. The bank cited rising life expectancy as one reason for the proposal. Average life expectancy in Tajikistan increased from 68.4 years in 2010 to 76.6 years in 2024. The country’s national development strategy aims to raise life expectancy to 80 years by 2030 — 78 years for men and 82 years for women. The ADB also suggested considering an increase in the minimum pension contribution period from 25 to 30 years for men and from 20 to 30 years for women. The report notes that women retire five years earlier than men and, on average, live longer, meaning they receive pensions for a longer period despite contributing for fewer years. Support Novastan, the European Central Asia magazine By supporting Novastan, you are supporting the only English, French and German-language media specialising in Central Asia. We’re independent and we need your help to stay that way! Support Novastan Just kilometres from Karakorum, the former capital of the Mongol Empire, archaeologists are uncovering evidence of thousands of years of human activity. Italian archaeologist Roberta Menegazzi speaks to Novastan Editor-in-Chief Mathieu Lemoine about discoveries in Mongolia’s Bayangolyn Valley, the technologies transforming archaeological research, and the importance of working with local communities to preserve the country’s cultural heritage. The ancient city of Karakorum, established under Genghis Khan in the 13th century, remains one of Mongolia’s most celebrated archaeological sites. Yet the surrounding Orkhon Valley holds traces of a much longer history, extending well beyond the rise and fall of the Mongol Empire. Around 14 kilometres northwest of modern Kharkhorin, the Bayangolyn Valley contains archaeological remains dating from the Bronze Age to more recent periods. These include funerary and ritual monuments, possible settlements and other structures that offer insights into how successive communities inhabited and shaped the landscape. Since 2018, the Italian Archaeological Mission in Kharkhorin, led by Roberta Menegazzi of the Centro Ricerche Archeologiche e Scavi di Torino per il Medio Oriente e l’Asia (CRAST), has worked with Mongolian institutions to research and promote the region’s archaeological heritage. The mission is funded by the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation. Read more on Novastan : “Heritage is something alive”: Ganzorig Miimaa reimagines Mongolia through photography Initially focused on heritage education and museum cooperation, the partnership expanded into field research in 2023. Working alongside the National University of Mongolia and the Kharakhorum Museum, the team has documented dozens of archaeological structures, employed advanced surveying technologies and begun excavations in the Bayangolyn Valley. In an interview with Novastan, Menegazzi discusses the mission’s findings, the importance of Italian-Mongolian scientific cooperation, and why archaeology should involve not only researchers but also the communities living alongside ancient sites. Italian archaeologist Roberta Menegazzi. Photo: CRAST. To begin with, how did the Italian Archaeological Mission in Kharkhorin come about? What initially attracted your team to this part of Mongolia, and how have the project’s objectives evolved since its launch in 2018? Our work in Mongolia actually began as a result of an agreement signed in 2016 between the cities of Turin and Kharkhorin, which recognised our institution (the Centro Ricerche Archeologiche e Scavi di Torino per il Medio Oriente e l’Asia – CRAST) as particularly well-placed to contribute to cultural and scientific cooperation. This agreement gave us the opportunity to establish a collaboration with Mongolian institutions, which officially started in 2018, when we signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the Kharakhorum Museum and the National University of Mongolia. Our initial goal was to help promote awareness and appreciation of the rich historical and archaeological heritage of the Kharkhorin area. In the beginning, our work focused mainly on educational programmes for school groups visiting the Kharakhorum Museum. We developed and tested educational activities and tools through training sessions involving museum staff, teachers, and people working in local cultural and social institutions. Over the years, this collaboration has grown stronger, and the mutual trust we have built with our Mongolian colleagues has opened up new opportunities. Professor Erdenebat Ulambayar of the National University of Mongolia and Bayaraa Terbish, Director of the Kharakhorum Museum, invited us to join their archaeological research in the region. This marked an important new stage in our collaboration, and in 2023 we began working together in the Bayangolyn Valley, about 14 kilometres northwest of modern Kharkhorin and the site of Karakorum, the first capital of the Mongol Empire. The Kharkhorin area is best known for Karakorum, the former capital of the Mongol Empire. What makes the Bayangolyn Valley particularly interesting for archaeologists, and what can studying this area tell us beyond the history of the imperial capital? The Bayangolyn Valley is characterised by a concentration of archaeological remains dating from the Bronze Age to modern times. Its archaeological potential has been recognised for almost a century, and over the past thirty years, it has attracted increasing scholarly attention. The valley is located close to two major historical sites: Karakorum, the capital of the Mongol Empire, and Karabalgasun, the capital of the Uyghur Empire. Studying this area can therefore help us better understand not only the long-term history of human occupation in the region, but also the relationship between these major political centres and their surrounding landscape. During your 2024 fieldwork, your team documented 39 archaeological structures in the Bayangolyn Valley. What kinds of structures did you identify, and were there any findings that particularly surprised you? Over the years, the Bayangolyn Valley has been investigated by several archaeological expeditions, including a Mongolian-German team that carried out extensive surveys across the wider Orkhon Valley. Previous research has focused on different areas and periods of occupation within the Bayangolyn Valley, providing an important foundation for our own work. Among the 39 archaeological structures we documented in the 2024 campaign, 29 are khirigsuurs – Bronze Age stone burial and ritual monuments found across Mongolia- , mostly located along the valley slopes and on the natural terraces overlooking it. Archaeological excavations in the Bayangolyn Valley. Photo: CRAST. These ritual monuments – generally consisting of a central stone mound surrounded by a square or circular enclosure of stones, often accompanied by multiple smaller satellite features – are among the most distinctive markers of the Bronze Age landscape in Mongolia. One aspect that particularly caught our attention was their concentration in the valley, a feature that had not emerged from previous reports. Your mission has employed drone surveys, multispectral imaging and digital terrain modelling to investigate archaeological remains. How have these technologies changed your understanding of the landscape? These technologies are particularly useful for studying archaeological landscapes, as they allow us to collect accurate, georeferenced data across large areas in a relatively short time. This is particularly true of fixed-wing drones, such as the one we used in our investigations in the Bayangolyn Valley. These tools are especially valuable in a country like Mongolia, where some archaeological remains are visible on the surface, as in the case of the khirigsuurs, while others lie just below ground level. Our survey – carried out in collaboration with the Department of Architecture and Design of the Politecnico di Torino – has provided us with detailed documentation of the archaeological features across the area under investigation, including both visible remains and traces of buried structures. This has given us a more comprehensive picture of the archaeological landscape in the Bayangolyn Valley and provided a solid basis for planning further investigations. Such documentation is valuable not only for archaeological research, but also for the protection and management of the cultural heritage of the area. Topographic surveying in the Bayangolyn Valley. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline. The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity. President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev has given an interview to the French Le Figaro newspaper. Trend presents the interview. -My first question would be Mr. President, why did you launch an offensive on September 27 against Nagorno-Karabakh? What are the political objectives of this military attack? -We did not launch military attack on Nagorno-Karabakh on September 27th. It was Armenia who launched a military attack on Azerbaijan, and in the first hours of this military attack we had victims, among civilians and among our military servicemen. This was the 3rd military provocation by Armenia against Azerbaijan, within 3 months. First, they attacked us on the state border between Armenia and Azerbaijan, far away from the Karabakh region. And by unanimous opinion of international observers it was Armenia who launched an attack on us. They wanted to occupy new territories. they wanted to take control over the strategic energy infrastructure which situated several kilometres from our state border with Armenia. As you probably know, Trans Adriatic Pipeline is almost completed. And the Southern Gas Corridor project is not only a project of energy security of Azerbaijan but also of Europe. We think that one of the goals of Armenia was to take control of that pipelines and to blackmail us, and maybe European consumers. They got a serious response. We pushed them back. But unfortunately, next month, in August, they send the sabotage group, which planned to commit acts of terror against Azerbaijanis. The head of the sabotage group was detected by our military people, military servicemen, and he gives evidence. So, it is a deliberate attempt to disrupt negotiations and to attack Azerbaijan. As far as political goals of Armenia, which they pursued launching the attack, was to keep the status quo unchanged, to put the blame for this escalation on us, to disrupt negotiations completely, and to involve third countries and to internationalize the conflict. We only gave them adequate response, as a result of that we liberated and continue to liberate part of the internationally recognized territory of Azerbaijan. -Azerbaijan has the mission to be a hub not only on energy pipelines but also on internet, fiberglass cables. And there is Azerbaijani company called Neqsol who want to be the connection between Europe and Central Asia, for internet. Do you think that this project is still possible or not to have directly through Azerbaijan in Internet from Europe, to Central Asia? -We as you correctly mentioned became already the regional hub for not only for energy, but also for transportation. We are now providing important transportation network for our partners across the Caspian in the eastern part of the Caspian Sea and Europe. Our investments in infrastructure resulted in creation of a very broad international cooperation format on transportation. Of course, everything started with the energy infrastructure, oil and gas pipelines going through Azerbaijan already became very important source of energy security. And with respect to the oil pipelines we already transit oil from Central Asia, through Azerbaijan to Europe. With respect to the internet connection, we invest largely into IT sector, internet penetration in Azerbaijan is about 80 percent. 80 percent of our population are internet users. And we have very developed private companies in this area. Therefore, the company which you mentioned as far as I know is a private company, which has its own agenda, and which invested in the region. How are the current military operations? -It is less than one month, and during this one month as a result of a very successful counter-attack, Azerbaijan managed to liberate part of the occupied territories, cities and villages and every day we report about new cities and villages which have been operated. It was not easy, because during the 30 years of occupation Armenia built on the occupied territories very solid engineering constructions. So, it was not easy to cross the line of contact. But we did it in different directions, in the north, in the south. And this demonstrates the high level of capacity, capability of Azerbaijani Army, and we defeat Armenia on the battlefield. And they have to run away from us. So, we already restored the international border with Iran. More than 130 km of this border was under occupation. So, we did a lot on the battlefield and this continues. Armenia two times violated the ceasefire. If they didn’t violate the ceasefire, first on the 10th of October brutally violated it launching a ballistic missile on the sleeping city of Ganja and second time on the 17th of October, today the clashes would have stopped and political solution would have prevailed. That’s our position. But they launched an attack on Ganja with ballistic missile on the 10th of October, first. Second, ballistic missile’s launch was made from the territory of Armenia. And you know, big countries can monitor it clearly. They know from where it is launched and what is a task for the missile? The task was to hit civilians. They hit the area of Ganja where people live. So, that was an act of international terror, that was another reflection of the war crime policy of Armenia. These attacks on Ganja, cannot be justified. And they will be responsible for that. -By accepting the intervention of Turkey and the arrival of Syrian fighters from Turkey, aren’t you afraid of turning local conflict into a regional war? -First of all, Turkey is not involved in the conflict at all. https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-us-satell.body: News US Accuses Russia Of 'Deliberately Reckless' Move With Military Satellite Flyby By Mike Eckel October 22, 2026 17:40 CET US Accuses Russia Of 'Deliberately Reckless' Move With Military Satellite Flyby Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Hundreds of commercial and military satellites fly in "low earth orbit," a crowded section of Earth's outer atmosphere. US officials publicly accused Russia of threatening a Finnish-operated commercial satellite that provides imagery and intelligence to Ukraine and other nations, calling the move "deliberately reckless." In response to the accusations, made during a United Nations debate on October 21, Russia broadly described US claims as "absurd" and accused Washington of its own "aggressive military space ambitions." SEE ALSO: Star Wars: A Russian Military Satellite Gets Very, Very Close To One Used By Ukraine The back-and-forth came days after a Russian military satellite known as Kosmos-2612 moved "dangerously" near to ICEYE-X36, a satellite registered in the United States and operated by a Finnish company called ICEYE. The Russian satellite came "exceptionally close" -- within 200 meters, by some estimates -- something that space officials and amateur satellite watchers said was extremely unusual. "This was not a routine conjunction or 'fly by,'" LeoLabs, an aerospace intelligence company, told RFE/RL. "The behavior is consistent with sophisticated rendezvous and proximity operations." A Russian Soyuz spacecraft approaches the International Space Station on December 21, 2012. ICEYE-X36 carries a radar technology that can gather detailed terrestrial images, even through cloud cover. The Finnish company in January signed a contract with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry to provide intelligence. Kosmos-2612 "exhibited threatening behavior by intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite," Brian Hardesty, an adviser to the US Delegation to the Conference on Disarmament, said during a meeting in New York of the UN First Committee, a body that debates arms control and disarmament issues. "These behaviors appear consistent with an on-orbit weapons operation." "The decision to conduct these activities was deliberately reckless," he said. Russia's representative who could not be immediately identified, did not directly address the assertion. "We call on member states to give the proper response to the aggressive military space ambitions of the United States," he said. He also referenced comments made last month by the secretary of the US Air Force, the top civilian official for that military branch. Speaking to a conference outside of Washington, Troy Meink's comments that Washington has in fact deployed actual weapons in space -- "on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action" -- caused a jolt among policy experts. Other longtime space watchers, however, said, the announcement merely stated publicly what had already been obvious for some time. "The United States did not suddenly weaponize space by acknowledging that it possesses these capabilities," wrote Mallory Stewart, a former top arms control secretary at the US State Department. "An arms race in space has been under way for years." https://www.rferl.org/a/serbia-vucic-bus.body: Serbia Exclusive: Rubio Receives Request To Sanction 4 Vucic-Linked Businessmen Ahead Of Serbia Elections By RFE/RL's Balkan Service October 22, 2026 22:36 CET Exclusive: Rubio Receives Request To Sanction 4 Vucic-Linked Businessmen Ahead Of Serbia Elections Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic (file photo) Four Serbian businessmen with close ties to the country's current government have been named in a request for US sanctions submitted to Secretary of State Marco Rubio by Republican Congressman Joe Wilson. The proposed sanctions target Ivan Bosnjak and Stojan Vujko of Millennium Team, Davor Macura of Alta Bank, and Zeljko Mitrovic, the owner of Pink TV. The request, submitted on October 14 and contained in a letter seen by RFE/RL, calls for the four men to be barred from traveling to the United States and from accessing the US financial system. Wilson addressed the letter to Rubio in his capacity as co-chairman of the Commission on Security and Cooperation in Europe, also known as the US Helsinki Commission. The letter accuses the four men of using public resources for personal enrichment and describes them as associates of Aleksandar Vucic, Serbia's former president and dominant political figure for more than a decade. "They sustain his corrupt regime, have worked to undermine US interests in the country and the region, and are actively involved in rigging the October 25 election," the letter says, referring to Serbia's upcoming parliamentary elections. A photo of the letter sent by Congressman Joe Wilson to Marco Rubio on October 14 Millennium Team and Alta Bank rejected the allegations in responses to RFE/RL, describing them as false, while Zeljko Mitrovic did not directly address the claims contained in the sanctions request. Neither Millennium Team nor Alta Bank has been subject to international sanctions, nor has Bosnjak, Vujko, or Macura. Mitrovic, however, was placed under US sanctions over his ties to the regime of the late Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic. Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party did not respond to RFE/RL's request for comment.' 'Multiple Corrupt Contracts' The snap elections are seen as the most uncertain yet for Vucic, who is seeking to return as prime minister after resigning as president on September 27. Having served two presidential terms, he is constitutionally barred from seeking a third. Vucic, who previously served as prime minister from 2014 to 2017, and his Serbian Progressive Party have dominated Serbian politics for the past 14 years. SEE ALSO: Could Vucic Become Serbia's Prime Minister Again? In response to a query from RFE/RL, the US State Department said it does not comment on its correspondence with Congress or on its actions in specific cases due to visa record confidentiality. "The Trump Administration is protecting our nation and our citizens by upholding the highest standards of national security and public safety through our visa process," the response said. The United States can impose sanctions on countries, companies, organizations, or individuals it determines pose a threat to its national security, foreign policy, or economy. Embed share Is Serbia's President Pulling A Putin-Medvedev Power Swap? by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:55 0:00 Direct link 240p | 4.4MB 360p | 6.4MB 480p | 9.3MB 720p | 14.7MB 1080p | 23.9MB Such measures are a foreign-policy tool and do not necessarily mean that those targeted have been convicted of a crime. The sanctions request alleges that Ivan Bosnjak and Stojan Vujko of the Millenium Company received "multiple corrupt government and Chinese contracts that ensure Western business, including American business, are pushed out of the country in favor of cronyism." The letter also says Alta Bank was "involved in the money laundering side of the business, while Pink TV consolidates the media and serves as the propaganda outlet." 'Kleptocratic Regime' Wilson accused Vucic of hollowing out the rule of law and attempting to dismantle democratic competition in Serbia. "He made many promises to the United States and delivered on none of them. Rather, his kleptocratic regime has invited in Russian and Chinese influence," the letter says. Wilson urged Rubio to take the proposed measures to "ensure that the Vucic regime cannot steal the election." Republican Congressman Joe Wilson (file photo) The US Helsinki Commission, which Wilson co-chairs, is an independent US government body that monitors compliance with international security and human rights commitments. According to its website, it promotes security by advancing human rights, democracy, and economic, environmental, and military cooperation in the 57 participating states of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE). 'Troubling Signs' Separately, several days before the parliamentary elections, a bipartisan group of US senators urged Serbian authorities to ensure a level playing field for all participants, saying they had observed "troubling signs" ahead of the vote. They said "reports of unlawful wiretapping of opposition members and attempts to discredit and undermine election observation missions are deeply concerning." SEE ALSO: US Lawmakers Target Serbia's Democratic Backsliding, Ties To Russia, China, Iran In a statement to RFE/RL, Alta Bank categorically rejected allegations that it, the Alta Group, or Davor Macura was involved in money laundering, corruption, the misuse of public resources, or electoral interference. "No competent authority in any jurisdiction has made any finding or decision of the kind alleged against Alta Bank, Alta Pay Group or Mr Macura," the bank's spokesperson said. They said Macura was not a politician but a private entrepreneur whose business interests span banking, payment services, and other sectors. They added that Alta Bank operates under the supervision of the National Bank of Serbia and applies the highest standards of anti-money-laundering controls and regulatory compliance. "The effectiveness of these controls and compliance systems has been confirmed repeatedly through internal and external audits," the spokesperson said. The bank added it had seen no evidence of a sanctions request being submitted to the US State Department and would seek clarification from the relevant authorities. Millennium Team, meanwhile, said it operates "transparently and in accordance with the law." "We do not comment on inaccurate and unfounded claims. If they are published, we will protect our rights by pursuing the legal remedies available to us," the company said. SEE ALSO: How Kremlin Propaganda Is Spreading Through Serbia Zeljko Mitrovic, owner of Pink Media Group, responded to RFE/RL's request for comment by sending a link to his Instagram post dated July 2, in which he congratulated the United States ahead of the country's Independence Day. "I am personally very happy that Serbia and America have entered a new era of rapid development of positive and friendly relations," he wrote. Mitrovic also referred to a "brief setback in relations" between Serbia and the United States in the late 1990s, describing that era as having been marked by "misunderstandings and a lack of mutual understanding." During that period, Mitrovic was placed on a US sanctions list over his ties to Milosevic's government and activities deemed to support it. The sanctions included a ban on entry into the United States, as well as a prohibition on business and financial dealings with American companies and individuals. At the time, he was also sanctioned by the European Union. Milosevic, the former president of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, died in custody at the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugosla

https://www.rferl.org/a/serbia-voting-vu.body: Serbia Serbia's Vucic Faces Biggest Election Challenge Yet Amid Fraud Fears By Iva Martinovic and Nevena Bogdanovic October 23, 2026 07:49 CET Serbia's Vucic Faces Biggest Election Challenge Yet Amid Fraud Fears Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Students wave flags during a march to Belgrade to support opposition candidates on October 19. After 14 years dominating Serbian politics, Aleksandar Vucic faces the biggest challenge to his rule in parliamentary elections on October 25 from an opposition movement that has sprung from mass student protests . But the campaign has been marked by growing concern about how fair the vote will be, with RFE/RL's Balkan Service uncovering some 500,000 people who were registered to vote without a full address -- raising fears of electoral fraud. Serbia's last election, in 2023, was followed by protests after international observers reported irregularities including bussing in voters from neighboring Bosnia-Hercegovina and voter intimidation. Vucic resigned as president in late September and, unable to run for a third term, is now aiming to be prime minister -- a role he held from 2012 until becoming head of state in 2017. Embed share Is Serbia's President Pulling A Putin-Medvedev Power Swap? by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:55 0:00 Direct link 240p | 4.4MB 360p | 6.4MB 480p | 9.3MB 720p | 14.7MB 1080p | 23.9MB His rule has been marked by a balancing act in which he has sought to foster good relations with Western nations while also cozying up to Russia and China. But Chinese investment has come at a political price. Tragedy At Novi Sad The election comes just days before the second anniversary of the Novi Sad tragedy. The deaths of 16 people when a renovated canopy at the city's railway station collapsed on November 1, 2024, triggered nationwide protests amid reports of corrupt practices at the construction site, a flagship government project led by Chinese businesses. The government denied this and the protests were met with police violence and arrests. One of the most serious incidents occurred on March 15, 2025, when authorities allegedly used an unlawful sonic weapon against peaceful demonstrators. Days after another student protest in June this year, Vucic announced he'd step down and hold early elections. Polling to date suggests Serbia's electorate is largely divided between those supporting a broad coalition built around the ruling party and those backing the student movement. "These are the first elections in more than a decade whose outcome is genuinely very uncertain," Vladimir Bilcik, a former European Parliament rapporteur for Serbia, told RFE/RL. The students have no formal leaders, and their electoral list is made up of nonpartisan figures, most of them university professors. Their candidate list is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, although they have said this does not mean he would become prime minister should they win. Serbian Students Hold Mass Rally Ahead Of Crucial Parliamentary Vote by RFE/RL No media source currently available 0:00 0:00:30 0:00 Fair Elections? The Serbian government says it has since implemented all recommendations made by the OSCE's election observation mission following its criticism of the 2023 election. This was contradicted in an interim report by the OSCE, which has 300 observers in Serbia to monitor voting. RFE/RL investigations have found irregularities at the very first stage of the electoral process: the voter register. RFE/RL found that more than half a million people listed in the register did not have a precise address recorded, lacking a street name or house number. SEE ALSO: US Lawmakers Target Serbia's Democratic Backsliding, Ties To Russia, China, Iran RFE/RL also found hundreds of registered voters listed at public facilities, including social welfare centers, and at houses that could not reasonably accommodate so many residents. These findings have drawn public scrutiny because election observers have previously raised suspicions that the authorities organized the "mass migration" of voters -- Serbian citizens from neighboring countries allegedly registered at addresses in Serbia to gain voting rights there, potentially benefiting the ruling party. RFE/RL investigations have also found that the number of eligible voters for Serbian elections in Bosnia and Kosovo increased ahead of the vote. Both are places where ethnic Serbs are considered an important pool of support for Vucic's Progressive Party. Four employees of institutions in Kosovo funded by Serbia have told RFE/RL they were being pressured to vote for the ruling party. Their identities or exact place of work cannot be revealed. In Serb-majority areas of Kosovo, various educational and healthcare institutions receive state funding from Serbia. Domestic election observers have documented similar practices at workplaces in several Serbian municipalities. The election is also taking place amid allegations of illegal surveillance and the arrest of government opponents, as Vucic has tightened his grip on the security services over his 14 years in power. A statement issued by the US Senate's Foreign Relations Committee on October 21 pointed to reports of illegal surveillance of opposition members and attempts to discredit and undermine election observation missions. Embed share Serbia Honors 'Butcher Of Bosnia' Ratko Mladic, Drawing Outrage Over Glorification by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:41 0:00 Direct link 240p | 4.8MB 360p | 7.0MB 480p | 10.2MB 720p | 16.6MB 1080p | 27.7MB Reporting by SHARE, a Serbian nonprofit focused on digital security, and researchers at Toronto University, alleged at least 16 cases of the Pegasus surveillance software -- which is illegal in Serbia -- being used in 2026. The opposition and students accuse the authorities of conducting the surveillance, while government officials deny spying on their opponents. Serbia has experienced a decline in freedoms over the past decade, a trend also noted in the latest report by international watchdog Freedom House. Between East And West Some US lawmakers have warned that Moscow could play an active role in Serbia's election, while the European Parliament has also raised concerns about Russian influence operations in the country. "Russia is making available its best resources, tactics, and methods to monitor, suppress, and disrupt the citizens of Serbia as well as the powerful student movement that wants to restore the rule of law in the country," Republican Congressman Joe Wilson told RFE/RL. Russian President Vladimir Putin has personally expressed his support for Vucic ahead of the election. During the election campaign, Vucic pledged to continue his foreign policy course, including his refusal to heed EU calls to impose sanctions on Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The student movement has focused its campaign on fighting corruption, putting foreign policy on the back burner. But it has also opposed sanctions against Russia and reiterated support for Belgrade's official position of refusing to recognize Kosovo's independence. Meanwhile, Serbia's EU integration has stalled , leaving the country -- once a front-runner alongside Montenegro -- near the back of the pack. No new chapter in Serbia's EU accession negotiations has been opened since late 2021. Democratic backsliding, unresolved relations with Kosovo, and refusal to impose sanctions on Russia are among the main reasons for the impasse. https://www.rferl.org/a/ukraine-cuts-chi.body: Ukraine Ukraine Cuts Chinese Drone Dependence, But Critical Gaps Remain By Matthew Fulco October 22, 2026 13:05 CET Ukraine Cuts Chinese Drone Dependence, But Critical Gaps Remain Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google A Ukrainian serviceman launching a drone in the Zaporizhzhya region on October 7 On October 17-18, Ukrainian forces launched more than 1,000 drones deep into Russian territory, striking major energy and industrial infrastructure in St. Petersburg and the Leningrad region. The bulk of that force was built on the FP-1 long-range strike platform developed by Fire Point, one of Ukraine's largest drone makers. The company produces 200-260 drones a day, with 90 percent of components sourced domestically and the rest drawn from European and allied country supply chains. Fire Point deliberately tries to avoid using parts from China, the world’s largest drone manufacturer. This marks a sharp departure from 2022, the first year of Russia’s full-scale invasion, when Ukraine relied almost entirely on Chinese components. While Ukraine has cut its Chinese imports sharply -- China accounted for just 28 percent of direct drone imports as of the end of August, according to Ukrainian customs data -- it still relies on Beijing for essential components that remain difficult to replace at the necessary scale and cost. The main reasons for Ukraine’s rapid transition to greater UAV (unmanned aerial vehicle) self-sufficiency are “capital and contracts,” said Catarina Buchatskiy, co-founder and analytics director of the Kyiv-based Serpens Center for International Security. Driven by war necessity and government defense-tech initiatives such as Brave1, Ukraine rapidly built a drone industry from the ground up. With demand high, firms were able to raise significant capital. They discovered, that in many cases, “it’s less efficient to import and managed to reinvest their own revenue into local manufacturing,” Buchatskiy said. Embed share Wounded Ukrainian Soldier Rescued From Front Lines By Aerial Drone by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:20 0:00 Because Ukraine “is using drones day in and day out, they are able to rapidly iterate on them,” Ali Javaheri, a senior emerging technology analyst at private markets data firm PitchBook in New York, said in an interview. “They’re not testing this stuff on some government property in Arizona. There’s a live battlefield.” China inadvertently accelerated Ukraine’s drone localization initiative with export restrictions imposed in 2023 (on long-range drones) and 2024 (on certain components). Though the export controls targeted both Ukraine and Russia -- China claimed it did not want its drones being used in warfare -- Moscow has barely been affected given its “no limits” partnership with Beijing. Chinese companies that bypass the restrictions to supply Russia with drone parts rarely face prosecution at home. Kyiv responded to those export restrictions by ramping up domestic production and sourcing from more reliable partner countries. Balancing Risks And Costs Ukraine, however, continues to rely on China for certain drone components. These include sensors and lenses for thermal cameras, battery cells, electric motor materials, and some microelectronics. “Alternatives exist, but, for now, the quantities are insufficient to supply millions of drones,” Olena Kryzhanivska, a Toronto-based defense analyst and author of the Ukraine Arms Monitor newsletter, told RFE/RL. When it comes to the raw materials used in these components, China is hard to replace. Case in point: China accounts for 60 percent of the world’s production of germanium, a critical mineral used in infrared optics and thermal camera lenses. Beijing has also imposed tight restrictions on germanium exports. It can produce these camera components at a much lower cost than European competitors. Similarly, China has weaponized its dominance of rare-earth magnets, a foundational component of modern drone motors. Since Ukraine -- and indeed Europe overall -- cannot yet produce the magnets at scale, Ukrainian drone manufacturers have had to get creative to circumvent Beijing’s export controls. They use third-party intermediaries or route shipments through multi-country supply chains. SEE ALSO: How Ukraine's Strikes On Data Centers Disrupted Taxis, Shopping, And Business In Russia And Beyond Europe is expected to reach commercial-scale rare earth magnet production by the early 2030s. However, analysts still expect that European magnets will be 15 percent to 30 percent pricier than China’s. “The ability to diversify hinges on the ability to source drone components outside China at a cost that makes it sustainable,” emerging technology analyst Javaheri said. Within the Ukrainian defense industry, some insiders say that Ukraine can tolerate continued dependency on China given the urgency of its security needs. “The Ukrainians do not care if they are using Chinese parts. They just want to get things in the air,” said a defense industry executive speaking anonymously at a recent closed-door event in the US. Collaborating With Taiwan To further reduce its dependence on China for drone components, Ukraine is cultivating partnerships with democratic countries. Among them, Taiwan stands out for combining advanced manufacturing acumen -- it is the world’s largest producer of semiconductors -- with a shared strategic need with Ukraine to build supply chains free of Chinese inputs. According to Taiwan’s state-funded Research Institute for Democracy, Society, and Emerging Technology (DSET), Ukrainian companies use Taiwanese flight controllers, batteries, motors, cameras, and other microelectronic components. More recently, their interest in Taiwan-made drone components has expanded to sensors, single-mode optical fiber, and jet engines. In May, a delegation from Ukrainian drone association IRON, led by chief executive Volodymyr Cherniuk, visited Taiwan to meet with potential business partners. Thunder Tiger, one of Taiwan’s most prominent UAV manufacturers, has sent drone systems to Ukraine for field-testing and evaluation. Kunway Technology, another Taiwanese drone company, already exports two different models to Ukraine via Poland. Potential exists for more closely intertwined production between Taiwan and Ukraine, but several issues must be resolved first. On the one hand, “Ukraine-Taiwan co-production remains nascent because Taiwan's drone industry is still relatively nascent,” Michael Cunningham, a senior fellow in the China program at the Stimson Center in Washington, told RFE/RL. Taiwan exported about 242,000 drones in the first half of 2026, according to its Economy Ministry. During that same time period, Ukrainian defense agencies built and deployed nearly 2.5 million drones. Political considerations limit cooperation as well, given Ukraine’s lack of diplomatic relations with Taipei and Beijing’s hypersensitivity about Taiwan-related matters. “Ukraine's relationship with China is particularly delicate, not only because China is Ukraine's largest trading partner and could do serious economic damage if it wanted to but also because of Beijing's close partnership with Russia,” Cunningham said. “This gives Ukraine incentive to try to reduce dependency on China, but it has to be smart about how it does this.” Embed share Geran-4 Unpacked: What Makes Russia's New Jet-Powered Drone So Dangerous? by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:04:12 0:00 The need for low-key defense cooperation between Kyiv and Taipei may explain why 93 percent of Taiwan’s drone exports in the first half of the year went to Poland and the Czech Republi

https://www.rferl.org/a/tajikistan-asadu.body: Tajikistan Deportations And Jail Terms Leave Tajik Dissidents In Europe Fearing For Their Future By RFE/RL October 22, 2026 19:02 CET Deportations And Jail Terms Leave Tajik Dissidents In Europe Fearing For Their Future Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Representatives of the Tajik opposition organization Group 24 hold a protest rally in Germany. After Berlin deported a Tajik dissident back to his homeland in June, many others in the country fear they too may be forcibly returned to Tajikistan. (file photo) Listen to this article 6 min This audio is automated Learn more A Tajik opposition activist who was deported from Germany in June, has been sentenced to 17 years in prison on charges that include online calls for extremism, according to two sources in Dushanbe who spoke to RFE/RL on condition of anonymity. Asadullo Boboev, a 54-year-old member of the Europe-based opposition Reforms and Development of Tajikistan movement, is the latest Tajik opposition figure to be deported from abroad and sentenced to a lengthy prison term in Dushanbe. Other activists deported from Germany, Austria, and Poland have also been imprisoned after their return to Tajikistan in recent years, leaving fellow exiled dissidents fearful for their safety and increasingly doubtful that Western governments still support their struggle for democratic change. Two Tajik opposition figures living in Europe told RFE/RL that Boboev's case had intensified their anxiety about being forcibly returned to Tajikistan. But they also described a deeper sense of disillusionment, saying that the deportation of political opponents from European countries has undermined their confidence in the protection they once expected from the West. SEE ALSO: 'Real Journalism Is Dying' -- Tajikistan's War On Independent Media "It discourages the opposition when someone is deported from a democratic European country and then brutally sentenced,” said Farhod Odinaev, a member of the Islamic Renaissance Of Tajikistan -- the former Islamic Renaissance Party of Tajikistan (IRPT). "This shows that no country is protecting Tajik opposition members, and it will discourage them in their struggle," he said. Tajikistan's government has long pursued a brutal crackdown on its political opponents. The IRPT and another leading opposition movement, Group 24, have been banned and labelled terrorist organizations. Several officials, members, and supporters of both movements languish in Tajik prisons on extremism-related charges, while dozens have left the country fearing persecution. Opposition figures and rights advocates have repeatedly disputed the government's accusations against political activists, saying they are used to silence dissent. In its most recent country report on human rights practices , published in August 2025, the US State Department said it opposes the forced return or extradition of Tajik political dissidents as it sees it as part of a campaign of "transnational repression" by the Central Asian nation's government. Left On Their Own A former Tajik university professor who spoke to RFE/RL on condition of anonymity said the deportation cases reflected what he saw as a broader retreat by Western governments from supporting democratic change in countries such as Tajikistan. "In the recent past, Western governments and organizations provided political backing to the opposition," he said. SEE ALSO: As Tajik Activist Faces German Deportation, Exiles Fear They're Next Governments in Central Asia understood that crackdowns on political opponents, independent media, and protests could damage their relations with Western countries, he added. "That is not the case anymore,” said the former professor, who is based in Russia. “Opposition activists might feel that they are left on their own." Deported Despite Warnings Boboev was deported from Germany along with his 19-year-old son over their expired residency permits, despite warnings that he could face persecution if returned. Human Rights Watch criticized the deportation , warning that Boboev faced the risk of detention and mistreatment in Tajikistan. “Boboev’s criticism of the Tajik government made him a clear target,” said Hugh Williamson, the watchdog's Europe and Central Asia director. He called on Berlin to investigate the deportation and press Tajik authorities over Boboev's detention. Germany's opposition Left Party (Die Linke) also sought answers, submitting a parliamentary inquiry in September asking the government to explain Boboev's deportation. Asadullo Boboev (file photo) German authorities did not respond to RFE/RL's requests for comment at the time of the deportation in June. Boboev's wife and daughter were allowed to remain in Germany. His relatives later learned in August that he was being held at a detention facility run by Tajikistan's State Committee for National Security in Dushanbe. On October 19, sources familiar with the case told RFE/RL’s Tajik Service that a court in the Tajik capital had sentenced him to 17 years in prison on September 21. Tajik authorities have not publicly provided details of the case, and RFE/RL's attempts to contact court officials have been unsuccessful. SEE ALSO: Tajik Activist Reportedly Taken Into Custody Upon Arrival After German Deportation Boboev is the latest in a series of Tajik opposition activists deported from Europe and subsequently handed lengthy prison sentences. In 2024, Tajik activist Farrukh Ikromov was sentenced to 23 years in prison after being deported from Poland, while Bilol Qurbonaliev, a member of the banned Group 24 movement, received a 10-year sentence after his deportation from Germany in 2023. Hizbullo Shovalizoda, a member of the banned IRPT, was sentenced to 20 years after being deported from Austria in 2020. Dilmurod Ergashev, who was expelled from Germany in 2024, received an eight-year sentence. “We fear that the same thing could happen to any one of us,” said Hisomiddin Roziq, a Tajik opposition activist living in Warsaw. He added that Tajik authorities were pressuring his family to persuade him to return home. https://cpj.org/2026/10/azerbaijan-prose.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email London, October 22, 2026—Azerbaijan should drop its financial crimes case against two journalists and another staff member of Meclis.info, an independent media outlet covering the work of the country’s parliament, and stop using allegations of illegal funding from international donors to silence the independent press, the Committee to Protect Journalists said Thursday. On October 20, prosecutors in the capital Baku requested prison sentences of 12 years for Imran Aliyev , the founder of Meclis.info who has been jailed since 2024, and 11 years for the outlet’s data analyst Elgiz Gahraman on multiple economic crime charges linked to alleged violations of foreign funding laws. A third defendant, Meclis.info accountant Tamella Musayeva, was reportedly taken ill in the courtroom before prosecutors could request a sentence for her and the hearing was adjourned. Journalist Imran Aliyev reports on his April 18, 2024 arrest at Azerbaijan’s Baku International Airport. (Screenshot: CPJ/Abzas Media via Facebook) A verdict in the case is expected on November 3. “Azerbaijan’s authorities are using foreign funding laws to persecute news outlets in an unprecedented crackdown that has seen at least 25 journalists jailed for simply doing their jobs. The unjustifiable sentences requested for Imran Aliyev and Elgiz Gahraman of Meclis.info are yet another example of this,” said Fiona O’Brien, CPJ’s director for Europe and Central Asia. “European Court of Human Rights rulings against Azerbaijan have clearly stated that these types of charges are illegitimate and retaliatory. Azerbaijan must immediately release Aliyev and drop all charges against him and his colleagues.” Meclis.info is among four leading independent media outlets targeted over alleged unlawful receipt of funding from major Western donor organizations, amid a crackdown on Azerbaijani civil society and a decline in relations with the West. In July this year, authorities sentenced nine individuals linked to Toplum TV to prison terms of up to 15 years on similar allegations. In June 2025, six journalists and media workers from anti-corruption investigative outlet Abzas Media were jailed for up to nine years, and 12 journalists and media workers linked to Berlin-based Meydan TV are standing trial on a range of financial crime charges and remain in pretrial detention. Meclis.info publishes data-based analyses and video explainers on the work of Azerbaijan’s parliamentary deputies and has almost 100,000 followers across its social media accounts . Police arrested Aliyev, who is also chief executive of Meclis.info, on charges of currency smuggling in April 2024, amid a wave of detentions of prominent journalists on similar charges based on alleged Western funding. Aliyev said police beat and electrocuted him following his arrest. Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs denied the allegations. According to news reports, the charges filed against Aliyev and Gahraman are two counts each of illegal entrepreneurship and money laundering, tax evasion, forgery of documents, and use of forged documents. Musayeva was also charged with the same offences. She and Gahraman remain free, but under travel bans pending a verdict. Azerbaijani law requires civil society groups to obtain state approval for foreign grants and authorities say Meclis.info and other targeted outlets failed to comply. In rulings on similar cases , the European Court of Human Rights stressed that such an omission was punishable under Azerbaijani law by fines, not criminal sanctions . Independent experts say that authorities refuse to register independent organizations seeking foreign grants, making it impossible to legally receive funding from abroad. Azerbaijan was the world’s sixth-worst jailer of journalists in 2025, according to CPJ’s prison census . In addition to cases involving Western grants, multiple journalists have been jailed on separate charges. Authorities have also heavily restricted international media and sentenced exiled journalists to lengthy prison terms in absentia. https://cpj.org/2026/10/turkish-reporter.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email Istanbul, October 22, 2026—Turkish authorities must immediately free İsmail Arı, the latest journalist to be arrested in a relentless crackdown on independent media this year, and abolish the disinformation law that has supercharged these repressive tactics, the Committee to Protect Journalists said Thursday. “İsmail Arı has already spent more than two months in jail this year due to a baseless fake news claim. Enough is enough; he must be set free without delay,” said Özgür Öğret, CPJ’s Turkey representative. “As predicted from the day it was introduced, Turkey’s disinformation law is being used as a weapon against independent reporting and it should be abolished at once.” Ankara police summoned Arı, an Ankara-based reporter for the leftist daily BirGün, for questioning on October 20 after a complaint against him was filed by Ebubekir Şahin, the former chair of Turkey’s broadcasting regulator RTÜK . When he arrived to testify, Arı was taken into custody . A court arrested the journalist pending trial on October 21 on the suspicion of “publicly spreading disinformation” under Article 217/A of the Turkish penal code and “insulting a civil servant because of their duty” under Article 125/3-a. No court date has yet been set and Arı has yet to be indicted and formally charged. Arı was previously arrested in late March on suspicion of spreading “disinformation” and released pending trial on June 5. CPJ emailed Turkey’s Ministry of Justice for comment but did not receive an immediate reply. CPJ’s testimony outlines the devastating impact of the war on Sudan’s press, including killings, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances, sexual violence, displacement, and censorship, and highlights the critical role Sudanese journalists play in documenting atrocities and preserving evidence for accountability. https://www.azattyq.org/a/buu-bas-hatshy.body: ЖАҢАЛЫҚТАР БҰҰ бас хатшылығы: Қазақстан СІМ БАӘ ұсынған кандидатқа қолдау білдірді 23 қазан 2026 жыл, 10:55 БҰҰ бас хатшылығы: Қазақстан СІМ БАӘ ұсынған кандидатқа қолдау білдірді Бөлісу Сілтемесін көшіру Facebook X (Twitter) WhatsApp Email Бөлісу Бөлісу Сілтемесін көшіру Facebook X (Twitter) WhatsApp Email Бөлісу PDF VPN-сіз оқу Сайт бұғатталып тұрса да, материалды осы сілтемемен кіріп оқуға болады Google-да басымдық бер Қазақстан сыртқы істер министрлігі. Қазақстан Біріккен Араб Әмірліктерінің сыртқы істер министрі, БАӘ-нің БҰҰ жанындағы бұрынғы тұрақты өкілі Лана Заки Нусейбенің кандидатурасын БҰҰ-ның бас хатшысы лауазымына ұсынуды құптайды және осы бастаманы қолдайды. 22 қазанда Қазақстан сыртқы істер министрлігі осылай деп мәлімдеді. БАӘ БҰҰ хатшысы қызметіне елдің сыртқы істер министрі Лана Заки Нусейбені ұсынған еді. Қазақстан СІМ бейсенбі күнгі мәлімдемесінде БҰҰ бас хатшысының сайлауына халықаралық қауымдастықтың ерекше назар аударып отырғанын жазады. “Сайлау процесі Қауіпсіздік кеңесінде консенсусқа қол жеткізудегі белгілі бір қиындықтармен қатар жүріп отыр. Бұны бейресми дауыс берудің алдыңғы раундтарының нәтижелері куәландыруда. Осыған орай Қазақстан үміткерлер ортасының кеңеюін құптап, мұны сындарлы диалогты жалғастыру және өзара қолайлы шешім іздеу үшін қосымша мүмкіндік ретінде қарастырады” деп жазылған хабарламада. Қазіргі бас хатшы Антониу Гутерриштің өкілеті биыл 31 желтоқсанда аяқталады. Бұған дейін халықаралық БАҚ ресми кандидаттардың ешқайсысы Қауіпсіздік кеңесінің ортақ қолдауын әзірге ала алмай отырғанын, БҰҰ хатшысын таңдау тығырыққа тірелгенін жазған еді. Британдық The Guardian басылымы БҰҰ Бас хатшысы қызметіне ықтимал бейресми үміткерлер арасында Қасым-Жомарт Тоқаевты атаған. Қазақстан президенті Біріккен Ұлттар Ұйымындағы лауазымды қызметке бару ниеті жоқ екенін бірнеше рет қайталаған. Сарапшылар Тоқаевты БҰҰ Бас хатшысы лауазымына ұсыну нұсқасы Тоқаевтың өзіне көбірек қажет деп санайды. Сарапшылардың айтуынша, басты тартыс қазан-қарашадағы жабық дауыс беру процесінде өрбіп, негізгі үміткер желтоқсанда анықталуы мүмкін.
